Give the route of the double circulation and name each organ's vessels.

md: The heart is a muscular pump with four chambers. The two upper chambers, the **atria**, receive blood from the veins; the two lower ones, the **ventricles**, contract and pump it out. The **right** side sends blood to the lungs, the **left** side round the body, and a wall of muscle, the **septum**, keeps the two sides apart.

title: Why the left wall is the thickest
md: The left ventricle pumps blood all the way round the body, so it must build a higher pressure than the right ventricle, which pumps only as far as the nearby lungs. More muscle makes more pressure.

alt: A dissected sheep heart held in a hand and cut across below the atria, so both ventricles are open. On the left of the cut face a thick ring of dark muscle surrounds a small round cavity; on the right a much thinner wall surrounds a wide crescent-shaped cavity.
caption: A real sheep heart cut across: the round, thick-walled left ventricle beside the thin crescent of the right.
prompt: Which ventricle is which in this photograph, and what does the difference in wall thickness tell you about where each one has to pump?

stem: A heart is drawn from the front. Chamber X is a lower chamber on the right-hand side of the page, and its wall is the thickest in the heart. Explain how you can tell that X is (a) a ventricle and (b) the left ventricle. [2]

steps.working: (a) It is one of the two lower chambers.
steps.decision: The ventricles are the lower, larger chambers; the atria sit above them.

steps.working: (b) Its wall is thicker than the other ventricle's, and the right of the page is the person's left.
steps.decision: The thickest wall belongs to the chamber that pumps blood round the whole body.

prompt: A heart is drawn from the front. Chamber M is an upper chamber on the right-hand side of the page. Which chamber is it?
explain: Turn the diagram to face you, as the worked answer did: the right of the page is the person's left side, and an upper chamber is an atrium. So M is the left atrium.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because M is on the right of the page, but the heart faces you, so the right of the page is the person's left.
It tempts because the left ventricle is the chamber asked about most, but ventricles are the lower chambers and M is an upper one.

twin.prompt: Chamber N is a lower chamber on the left-hand side of the page, with a thinner wall than the other lower chamber. Which chamber is it?
twin.explain: The left of the page is the person's right, and a lower chamber is a ventricle. The thinner wall fits: the right ventricle pumps only to the lungs.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because N is on the left of the page, but the page's left is the person's right, and the left ventricle has the thicker wall.
It tempts because N is on the person's right, but the atria are the upper chambers and N is a lower one.

md: Every vessel is named by its direction. An **artery** carries blood **away** from the heart; a **vein** carries it **towards** the heart. What the blood carries plays no part in the name.

So the lung vessels are the two that surprise. The **pulmonary artery** carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs (there are two, one to each lung), and the **pulmonary vein** brings oxygenated blood back to the left atrium. The **aorta** leaves the left ventricle for the body; the **vena cava** brings blood back to the right atrium.

stem: Explain why the pulmonary artery is an artery, even though the blood inside it is deoxygenated. [2]

steps.working: It carries blood away from the heart, from the right ventricle to the lungs.
steps.decision: Start from where the vessel runs: out of the heart.

steps.working: A vessel is named by the direction of flow, not by its blood: away from the heart makes it an artery.
steps.decision: Then the rule itself, which is what the second mark is for.

prompt: Which vessel carries oxygenated blood towards the heart?
explain: Towards the heart makes it a vein, as the worked answer's rule said, and oxygenated blood comes from the lungs. The vein bringing it back from the lungs is the pulmonary vein.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because arteries are thought of as the oxygen carriers, but this one runs away from the heart, with deoxygenated blood.
It tempts because it does flow towards the heart, but its blood comes from the body and is deoxygenated.

twin.prompt: Which vessel carries oxygenated blood away from the heart?
twin.explain: Away from the heart makes it an artery, and oxygenated blood leaves from the left ventricle: the aorta. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood, and the pulmonary vein flows towards the heart.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because it is the other artery leaving the heart, but it carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs.
It tempts because it carries oxygenated blood, but it flows towards the heart, so it is a vein.

md: Follow one drop of blood from the body and back: **vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta**. On each side it enters an atrium, passes through a valve into the ventricle below, and leaves in an artery.
One full circuit of the body passes through the heart **twice**, once for each loop: a **double circulation**. Blood coming back from the lungs is pumped again before it sets off round the body.

stem:
Complete the route by naming the chamber or vessel in each numbered box. [4]
body → 1 → right atrium → 2 → pulmonary artery → lungs → 3 → left atrium → 4 → aorta

steps.working: Box 1: vena cava.
steps.decision: The vein that brings blood back from the body into the right atrium.

steps.working: Box 2: right ventricle.
steps.decision: From an atrium, blood passes through a valve into the ventricle on the same side.

steps.working: Box 3: pulmonary vein.
steps.decision: Back from the lungs towards the heart, so a vein.

steps.working: Box 4: left ventricle.
steps.decision: The left atrium passes blood down to the left ventricle, which pumps it into the aorta.

title: GCSE Biology Revision "The Heart and Circulation"
why: A second pass over the chambers and the route, now that you have worked it through yourself.

prompt: On one complete circuit of the body, how many times does the blood pass through the heart?
explain: Twice, as the worked route showed: once through the right side on the way to the lungs, once through the left side on the way to the body. That is what double circulation means.

twin.prompt: How many chambers of the heart does blood pass through between leaving the vena cava and entering the aorta?
twin.explain: The right atrium and the right ventricle, then, after the lungs, the left atrium and the left ventricle: four.

text: Valves and the heart's own supply

md: **Valves** keep the blood moving one way. One sits between each atrium and its ventricle, and one at the base of each artery leaving the heart, the aorta and the pulmonary artery. When the ventricles relax, the valves at the base of the arteries shut, so blood cannot fall back into the heart.

The heart muscle needs its own oxygen and glucose. The **coronary arteries** branch from the aorta and run over the outside of the heart; **coronary veins** drain it. If a coronary artery is blocked, the muscle beyond it is starved of oxygen.

stem: When the ventricles relax, which valves shut, and what does their shutting prevent? [2]

steps.working: The valves at the base of the aorta and the pulmonary artery shut.
steps.decision: Name the valves first: they sit at the start of the two arteries leaving the heart.

steps.working: They stop the blood in those arteries flowing back into the ventricles, so it moves one way.
steps.decision: Then the job: stopping backflow is the idea the mark is for.

prompt: The valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle does not close properly. When the left ventricle contracts, where does some blood leak?
explain: Locate the valve as the worked answer did: this one sits between the left atrium and the left ventricle. When the ventricle squeezes, blood meant for the aorta can also be pushed back through the gap into the left atrium.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because the ventricles sit side by side, but the septum keeps the two sides apart, whatever the valves do.
It tempts because the vena cava brings blood into the heart, but it joins the right atrium, on the other side of the septum.

twin.prompt: The valve at the base of the pulmonary artery does not close properly. When the right ventricle relaxes, where does some blood flow?
twin.explain: That valve should shut as the ventricle relaxes. If it cannot, blood in the pulmonary artery falls back into the right ventricle.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because the pulmonary artery leads to the lungs, but a leaking valve lets blood go backwards, not faster forwards.
It tempts because the ventricles lie side by side, but the septum keeps the two sides apart.

text: Every organ has its own pair

md: Every organ has an artery bringing blood **in** and a vein taking it **out**, named after the organ: **renal** for the kidney, **hepatic** for the liver, **pulmonary** for the lungs, **mesenteric** for the intestine. The arteries branch from the aorta; the veins lead back to the vena cava.
One vessel breaks the pattern. The intestine's veins do not lead back to the vena cava: they join the **hepatic portal vein**, which carries blood rich in digested food straight to the liver.

stem: For each vessel, name the organ it is joined to and say whether its blood flows into that organ or out of it. (a) the mesenteric artery (b) the hepatic vein (c) the pulmonary vein [3]

steps.working: (a) Into the intestine.
steps.decision: An artery brings blood in, and mesenteric means the intestine.

steps.working: (b) Out of the liver.
steps.decision: A vein takes blood out, and hepatic means the liver.

steps.working: (c) Out of the lungs, back to the heart.
steps.decision: Pulmonary means the lungs; a vein leaves the organ for the heart.

prompt: Which vessel takes blood out of the kidneys?
explain: Out of an organ means a vein, as the worked answer read each name, and renal means the kidney. So blood leaves the kidneys in the renal vein.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because renal is the right organ, but an artery brings blood into the kidney.
It tempts because it is a vein leaving an organ, but hepatic means the liver.

twin.prompt: Which vessel brings oxygenated blood to the liver?
twin.explain: Into an organ, with oxygenated blood from the aorta, means the artery: the hepatic artery. The hepatic portal vein brings blood from the intestine, and the hepatic vein takes blood away.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because it also carries blood into the liver, but its blood comes from the intestine and has given up oxygen there.
It tempts because hepatic is the right organ, but the hepatic vein takes blood out of the liver.

md: During exercise the muscles contract more, so they respire faster to release more energy. They need oxygen and glucose delivered faster, and their extra carbon dioxide taken away, so the heart beats faster and the **pulse rate** rises. It stays raised for a while after the exercise stops.
The pulse is each heartbeat felt in an artery near the skin, at the wrist or the neck, so counting it measures the heart rate.

stem: Describe how a student should measure her resting pulse rate. [3]

steps.working: Sit still for a few minutes first, so the pulse settles at its resting rate.
steps.decision: Resting means resting: a pulse taken straight after moving is still raised.

steps.working: Press two fingers, not a thumb, on the artery at the wrist and count the beats for 15 seconds, then multiply by 4.
steps.decision: A thumb has a pulse of its own; 15 seconds times 4 gives beats per minute.

steps.working: Repeat twice more and take the mean.
steps.decision: Repeats smooth out a miscount.

prompt: A student counts 21 beats at her wrist in 15 seconds. What is her pulse rate, in beats per minute?
explain: Scale 15 seconds up to a minute, as step 2 of the worked answer did: 21 × 4 = 84 beats per minute.

twin.prompt: He counts 19 beats in 15 seconds. What is his pulse rate, in beats per minute?

text: Cardiac output, and what training does

md: **Cardiac output** is the volume of blood the heart pumps in one minute: **cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate**, where the stroke volume is the volume pumped out in one beat. Multiply, because one stroke volume leaves the heart on every beat.

Regular exercise **strengthens the heart muscle**, so it pumps more blood in each beat and needs fewer beats at rest: a fit person's resting pulse is lower. The specification's words for the benefit are **increased cardiac output when at rest**; CCEA's 2019 scheme also accepted 'pumps more blood per beat'.

stem:
At rest, a student's stroke volume is 60 cm³ and her heart rate is 80 beats per minute.
(a) Calculate her cardiac output. [2]
(b) During a run her cardiac output rises to 12 000 cm³ per minute. Calculate the percentage increase. [3]

steps.working: (a) 60 × 80 = 4800 cm³ per minute
steps.decision: Multiply: one stroke volume on every beat, and 80 beats in a minute.

steps.working: (b) increase = 12 000 − 4800 = 7200 cm³ per minute
steps.decision: Find the increase before any percentage.
Divide by the value she started from, the resting output.

prompt: A man's stroke volume is 90 cm³ and his heart rate is 58 beats per minute. What is his cardiac output, in cm³ per minute?
explain: Multiply, as the worked answer did at rest: 90 × 58 = 5220 cm³ per minute. Adding the two numbers gives nothing meaningful: they are different kinds of quantity.

twin.prompt: A cyclist's stroke volume is 85 cm³ and his heart rate is 62 beats a minute. Work out his cardiac output in cm³ per minute.

md: **Label a valve, or name an organ.** When a question says label *a* valve, draw one line to one valve: in Summer 2024 a few labelled every valve. On a body plan, match each organ to its vessels: in Summer 2025 brain and intestine were the commonest wrong answers where the lungs and a kidney were meant.

**Who is fittest?** With three people, compare each measure with both of the others: 'the lowest of the three', never just 'low'. Remember the resting rate: on a Unit 1 breathing graph in March 2026, fewer candidates gave the lower resting rate as evidence of fitness.

stem: Three runners, P, Q and R, did the same exercise; the graph shows their pulse rates before, during and after it. R is the fittest. Use the graph to support this. [3]

steps.working: R's resting pulse is the lowest of the three: 60, against 70 for Q and 80 for P.
steps.decision: A fitter heart pumps more per beat, so it needs fewer beats at rest; state it against both others.

steps.working: R's pulse during the exercise is the lowest: 120, against 140 and 150.
steps.decision: The same reason holds while exercising: fewer beats move the blood the muscles need.

steps.working: R's pulse is back to resting quickest: 6 minutes after stopping, against 12 for Q and 16 for P.
steps.decision: Recovery is a length of time, measured from when the exercise stopped, at 10 minutes.

prompt: Runner S has a resting pulse of 58, T has 64 and U has 71. Which sentence earns the mark for 'S is the fittest'?
options: S has the lowest resting pulse of the three
S has a low resting pulse
answer: S has the lowest resting pulse of the three
explain: Compare with both of the others, as each worked line did. 'The lowest of the three' puts S below T and U; 'low' or a true fact that fits all three does not.

optionNotes.option: S has a low resting pulse
optionNotes.why: It tempts because it is true, but 'low' on its own does not compare S with T and U, and the mark is for the comparison.
It tempts because it is true, but so are T's and U's, so it does not single S out.

twin.prompt: V's pulse is back to resting 4 minutes after exercise, W's after 7 and X's after 9. Which sentence earns the recovery mark for 'V is the fittest'?
options: V's pulse returns to resting quickest of the three
V's pulse returns to its resting rate
twin.answer: V's pulse returns to resting quickest of the three
twin.explain: Only 'quickest of the three' compares V with both W and X; 'quickly' and 'returns' say nothing about the other two.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because it sounds like the answer, but 'quickly' does not compare V with W and X.

optionNotes.option: V's pulse returns to its resting rate
optionNotes.why: It tempts because it describes recovery, but every runner's pulse returns, and the mark is for being quickest.
